top.line: Stop sharing keys: move every secret by public key
top.para: secrets.sgit.ai began on 5 October as a passkey-unlocked password manager whose app was never built; its passkey work became the newsroom's reader vault. It now becomes a service for moving a secret from A to B. Shared easy keys proved broken, so every person, browser and agent gets a key pair.

in-short.line: Public keys replace broken shared keys across eight scenarios
in-short.para: The easy shared keys were broken, so everything moves to public keys and secrets.sgit.ai becomes the service. Eight scenarios cover people, agents, browsers, devices and teams. The private key sits in a vault wrapped by passkey PRF bytes, most plumbing exists, and capabilities are charged for while one secret stays free.

today.line: A careful site with sharing designed, no app
today.para: Created on 5 October and at v0.1.13 by 6 October, the site has a reality page of 75 claims, 42 shipped, 28 proposed and 5 deliberately absent. The site, pipeline, labs and review tools shipped; the app did not. Its planned phase 2 key-pair sharing scheme now becomes the product.

no-keys.line: The friendly two-word codes were cryptographically broken
no-keys.para: The sgit team's 6 August review found two-word codes carry 30.2 bits, with a public id that is an unsalted hash of the token and a fixed salt, so one precomputed table opens every vault. Creating them was disabled in June. Public keys remove the need to move a secret key at all.

scenarios.line: Eight cases, from QR requests to agents and teams
scenarios.para: Request a secret by sharing a public key as a link or QR code; give one via a signed directory; send to an agent session, tested end to end, or a scheduled agent's append-lane inbox. A non-exportable browser key survived a restart. New devices pair by QR, sgit pki works serverless, and teams get per-member inboxes.

vault.line: A passkey-unlocked vault holds the private key, not managers
vault.para: Each person's key pair lives in an identity vault unlocked through the WebAuthn PRF extension, with a 26-character, 128-bit recovery code. Password managers keep the passkey: Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello, Firefox and Bitwarden support PRF, while LastPass is unconfirmed. PasswordCredential is not Baseline, so not a foundation.

build.line: The plumbing exists; the product and directory do not
build.para: SG/Send already does one-time drops with download limits and expiry, append lanes act as write-only inboxes tested with a hundred writers, and sgit pki makes and signs with RSA-4096 and ECDSA keys. Missing are request objects, a signed directory, a shared envelope format and a new client.

commercial.line: Sending one secret is free; capabilities are charged for
commercial.para: Following the newsroom's pay-after-value model, sending and opening a single secret is free. Charges apply to the identity vault and recovery, the directory and verified fingerprints, device and agent pairing, team inboxes with audit, and integrations. They apply even when bytes bypass the servers, since the value is identity and workflow.

brief.line: Refactor the site so public-key sharing is product one
brief.para: The agent should keep the pipeline and labs but lead with sharing. That means no short codes, one signed envelope format for JavaScript and sgit pki, request links and QR codes, a PRF-wrapped identity vault, a signed directory, agent pairing, server changes that never see private keys, password manager integrations, and free single secrets.

limits.line: Nothing is built, tests were local, pricing proposed
limits.para: The service does not exist: secrets.sgit.ai is a site with a design and no app. The tests ran on one machine with Chromium, a local SG/Send server and dummy secrets. LastPass PRF support was not found, and nothing is charged today.

sources.line: Sources: the secrets site, SG/Send API, review and specifications
sources.para: Drafted from a voice memo of 15 October 2026. The agent read SGit-AI__Website__Secrets and its reality page, the SG/Send transfer API and the sgit team's review of two-word codes, and ran browser and command-line tests. External sources are W3C Web Authentication Level 3 and MDN on PasswordCredential.
